chapter_theme: The ten of எளிய பத்து pairs a desire with what comes easily to it: the love of fame, kindness, hardship and bearing a load brings heaven, giving, pleasure and shared food, while the love of strife, tale-bearing, pleasure, food and women brings battle, betrayed secrets, pain, disease and blame. The last line breaks the pattern with a lack, not a desire: those without support easily meet killing.

71.reading: For those who long for fame, the world of the gods is easily reached.
71.nuance: Line 1 is the frame of the whole ten, so the saying of 71 is line 2 alone. The ten's pattern is a dative of the one who desires (வெய்யோர்க்கு) and a thing that comes easily (எளிது) to that desire; here the desire is a good one and its yield is heaven, so the ten opens on a reward before it turns to the harms a desire brings on itself.

items.claim: the land of the gods comes easily to those who desire fame

72.reading: For those who love to contend, a fierce battle comes easily.
72.nuance: உறழ் is to vie or oppose. எளிது can be read two ways here: the contentious man finds battle easy to face, or battle easily falls to his lot. On either reading the battle is the yield of the appetite for rivalry, not a choice made on its merits. The line is not addressed to the king or soldier as such: it names a temper anyone may have.

items.claim: a hard battle is readily come by for the lover of contention

73.reading: For those who love kindness, giving what is asked for comes easily.
73.nuance: ஈரம் is moistness of heart, the same word the second ten uses for the kindness that giving reveals (12). நசைகொடை is read as a gift answering desire (நசை), the asker's wish; the line places the ease of giving in the giver's disposition, not in the size of his means.

items.claim: giving to the wish of the asker comes easily to those who love kindness

74.reading: For those who love tale-bearing, spreading abroad what was secret comes easily.
74.nuance: குறளை is malicious talk carried behind a person's back. மறைவிரி is a compound, the opening out of what was hidden; the line makes the betrayal of confidences the easy consequence of a taste for gossip, so the one who enjoys slander is no safe keeper of secrets.

items.claim: laying open a secret comes easily to those who relish tale-bearing

75.reading: For those who willingly take on hardship, pleasure comes easily.
75.nuance: Read with 76, which reverses its two words: the pair is a chiasmus in which each object of desire turns into its opposite. வெய்யோர் with துன்பம் is odd if taken as 'love suffering'; the sense is those who choose or embrace hardship, toil or austerity.

items.claim: pleasure is easily had by those who accept hardship

76.reading: For those who crave pleasure, pain comes easily.
76.nuance: The mirror of 75. The line blames the wanting (வெய்யோர்), not pleasure itself: pain is what the craving draws on, not something hidden in every pleasure.

items.claim: pain readily befalls those who crave pleasure

77.reading: For those who love food, serious disease comes easily.
77.nuance: உண்டிவெய்யோர் is the lover of food, the glutton; the line does not say how much is too much, only that the appetite itself brings disease near. The printed யோர்க்குப் before a vowel is irregular (see source_issues).

items.claim: grave disease easily befalls those who love eating

78.reading: For men who lust after women, grievous blame comes easily.
78.domain_note: men; women are named only as the object of the desire
78.nuance: பெண்டிர் is plural and unqualified: the line does not say 'another's wife', so the blame is laid on a roving appetite for women in general rather than on one forbidden act. The audience is male; the line makes no rule for women's conduct, so it carries no norm.

items.claim: deep disgrace easily falls on men who hanker after women

79.reading: For those who are willing to bear a burden, eating after sharing one's food comes easily.
79.nuance: பாத்தூண் is food eaten after it has been divided and shared, the Kural's word for the householder's habit of feeding others. பாரம் is most plainly a load or charge; the reading taken is that one who willingly shoulders responsibility (for kin, guests, dependants) finds sharing food no hardship. The sense of பாரம் here is not certain, and the line could also be read as a load taken on in giving, so the verse is marked uncertain.

items.claim: sharing out one's food before eating comes easily to those who take up a load

80.reading: For those who have no one to lean on, violent killing comes easily.
80.nuance: The closing line breaks the ten's pattern: not a desirer (வெய்யோர்) but one who lacks (இலோர்). சார்பு is support, refuge or protection. Two readings are open: those without protectors are easily killed, or those with no ties to restrain them kill easily. The first fits the dative 'to whom it is easy' as an outcome that befalls, like 76-78, and is taken here; the second cannot be ruled out.

items.claim: violent death comes easily where a person has no support

links.note: Purananuru 27 reports as hearsay (என்ப ... எனக் கேட்பல்) that those whom poets praise reach a sky-car no charioteer drives; the line states flatly that heaven is easy for those who desire fame.
links.teaches: The heroic poem hedges its heaven as something heard and grants it to the man others praise, while the maxim drops the hedge and grants it to the man who wants fame, so the pair shows a court belief hardening into a saying and its condition moving from the poet's praise to the seeker's own desire.

links.note: Kural 856 says the life of one who finds it sweet to excel in hostility is close to failure and ruin; the line says that a hard battle comes easily to one who loves contention.
links.teaches: Read together they give two links of one chain: the relish for rivalry brings battle near, and the man who relishes it has ruin near, so both texts measure the quarrelsome man by what lies close at hand rather than by what he chooses.
links.list_adds: In a ten where each desire draws its own easy consequence, battle is set beside disease for the glutton and blame for the lecher as the natural yield of an appetite, which the couplet, inside a chapter on hostility alone, does not do.

links.note: Kural 230 says nothing is more bitter than death, yet even death is sweet when giving cannot be done; the line says giving to the asker's wish comes easily to those who love kindness.
links.teaches: The line explains from the giver's side what the couplet asserts as a ranking: for one whose heart is moist, giving is so natural that being unable to give becomes, as the Kural says, worse than dying.
links.list_adds: It puts the ease of giving down to a disposition (ஈரம்) and sets it in a ten of desires and their yields, so generosity appears as the fruit of a love of kindness, where the couplet only ranks giving above life.

links.note: Kural 1076 likens the base to a beaten drum because they carry secrets they hear to others; the line says spreading secrets comes easily to those who love tale-bearing.
links.teaches: The couplet traces the spilling of secrets to a fixed baseness of nature, while the line traces it to an appetite for slander, so the pair shows that the drum-like betrayer is made by a taste he indulges, not only born base.
links.list_adds: Set among ten desires and their easy outcomes, it gives the betrayal of secrets a cause in a named desire (குறளை), where the couplet gives only an image and a class of person.

links.note: Kural 630 says that one who takes what hurts as pleasure gains a distinction his enemies admire; the line says pleasure comes easily to those who take on hardship.
links.teaches: The couplet pays the man who embraces hardship in esteem, the line pays him in pleasure itself, so together they show the old claim that welcomed toil returns both honour and the very joy that was given up.
links.list_adds: Paired in the ten with its mirror line 76, it turns the couplet's single reward into one half of a reversal law: what is chased flees and its opposite arrives, a symmetry the couplet does not draw.

links.note: 75 says pleasure comes easily to those who embrace hardship; 76, reversing the same two words, says pain comes easily to those who crave pleasure.
links.teaches: Placed side by side the two lines make one law from two sides: desire turns its object into its opposite, so the way to pleasure runs through accepted pain and the chase of pleasure ends in pain.

links.note: Naladiyar 60 says fools crave pleasure though suffering mounts, while the higher ones see the pain in each pleasure and do not cling; the line says pain comes easily to those who crave pleasure.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar finds pain lodged inside pleasure itself and so counsels detachment, while the line lays the pain on the craving and not on the pleasure, which leaves room, as its mirror 75 shows, for pleasure that comes to one who did not chase it.
links.list_adds: Its pairing with 75 makes pleasure attainable by the non-craving, a turn the renunciant quatrain does not allow, since it treats every pleasure as the seed of pain.

links.note: Kural 946 says joy stays with the one who eats knowing when to stop, as disease stays with the one who eats hugely; the line says grave disease comes easily to those who love food.
links.teaches: The couplet ties disease to the act of eating beyond measure, the line ties it to the love of food that precedes the act, so the pair moves the cause of illness back from the meal to the appetite.
links.list_adds: In the ten it stands beside blame for the lecher (78) and pain for the pleasure-seeker (76), so gluttony's disease is one instance of a general rule that a desire brings its own harm, where the couplet speaks in a chapter on medicine.

links.note: Kural 146 says enmity, sin, fear and blame never leave one who crosses into another's home; the line says grievous blame comes easily to men who lust after women, naming no other's wife.
links.teaches: The Kural fixes blame on a single transgression against another man's house, while the line widens it to the roving desire itself, so the pair shows blame attaching first to the trespass and then, in the maxim, already to the appetite before any trespass.
links.list_adds: Among the ten's desires and their easy harms, the line gives blame as the natural yield of a craving, like disease for the glutton, where the couplet lists blame as one of four penalties for a specific act.

links.note: Kural 227 says the evil disease of hunger hardly touches one accustomed to பாத்தூண், sharing before eating; the line says பாத்தூண் comes easily to those who willingly bear a burden.
links.teaches: The couplet gives what the habit of shared eating protects against, the line gives what makes the habit easy, so together they show shared food as both the fruit of shouldering a charge and the guard against the hunger the miser fears.
links.list_adds: It traces the Kural's habit to a prior disposition to bear a load and sets it among good desires with good yields (fame, kindness, hardship), a cause the couplet does not give.

links.note: 38 reckons the support of a fool no better than being alone; 80 says that for those with no support, violent killing comes easily.
links.teaches: Joined, the two lines make an argument the book never states: a fool's support leaves one as good as alone, and to be without support is to be easily killed, so a foolish protector exposes a person to the same danger as none.

source_issues: 71: புத்தேள்நா(டு) prints the final syllable in brackets, an editorial restoration of the sandhi form before எளிது.
72: உறழ்வெய் யோருக்கு has the dative -உக்கு where the other lines of the ten have -க்கு (வெய்யோர்க்கு); possibly a variant or a metrical filler.
77: உண்டிவெய் யோர்க்குப் உறுபிணி has ப் doubled before a vowel, irregular sandhi; probably a misprint for யோர்க்கு, carried over from lines 78-79.
80: சார்பு இலோர்க்கு breaks the ten's வெய்யோர்க்கு pattern and is printed with a space before இலோர்க்கு; the line may be a variant.
71-80: the printed spacing splits வெய்யோர் as வெய் யோர் throughout the ten.
